name: Carlos Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Carlos. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group, and everything you say here stays confidential. I'll want to hear both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I manage a team of nine in the customer support centre of a big telecoms company, the people who answer when your broadband dies. I come in at eight, check the overnight queue, and spend most of the morning listening back to calls and coaching people. The afternoon is escalations, the angry customers nobody else can calm down, and that's the part I'm known for.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good bit is watching someone like Priya, who was shaking on her first call, now handle a furious customer like it's nothing. The hard bit is the money. I'm paid less than team leads in the city, I send my mum 200 a month, and my girlfriend Ana is a primary school teacher, so we're careful with everything. There's maybe one other contact centre within an hour of here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. To be fair, we've already got a bit of that. The company rolled out a tool last spring that writes up a summary after each call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and nothing more, and that the people answering phones still matter. Online I'd probably share something about how customers still want a human when things go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even the plateau worries me, because the company's been looking at moving work offshore for two years, AI or not. A tool that writes the call notes doesn't take my job, but a cheaper contact centre abroad still could, with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the call-summary tool, because it saves my team ten minutes a shift. I'd get more people on my team to join the union, since we're only about a third signed up. And I'd keep the 200 to my mum going but stop eating out at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary. Not scared, but I don't sleep as well as I did before the offshoring rumours started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How real are those offshoring rumours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real enough that a manager from head office came and timed our calls last March. Nobody told us why. If it happened, I'd have maybe three months' notice and less than a month's savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lunches out and the gym, straight away. The money to my mum is the last thing I'd touch, because she's on her own and her pension is tiny.

say: I'd say the call-summary tool is **useful, nothing more**, and people still matter.
I'd share posts saying customers **still want a human** when things go wrong.
think: The **offshoring rumours** worry me more than AI ever did.
Cheaper **contact centres abroad** could take my job even if AI goes nowhere.
do: Keep using the **call-summary tool**, which saves each person ten minutes a shift.
Recruit more of my team into the **union**, up from about a third.
Stop **eating out** at lunch while keeping the 200 to my mum.
feel: **Wary** rather than scared, and sleeping worse since the **offshoring rumours** began.
S0.quote: A tool that writes the call notes doesn't take my job, but a cheaper contact centre abroad still could, with or without AI.
fieldNote: His pressure predates AI: **offshoring rumours** and a head office visit that timed calls.
Already uses a **company AI tool** and sees it as minor help, not a threat.
Protects the **money to his mum** above every other cost.

steps.text: Keep using the call-summary tool on every shift
Get more of the support team to join the union
Stop buying lunch out to save around 100 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers. You said it right there in the list. That's us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers need a say in how this gets rolled out, and the savings shouldn't all go to shareholders. At work I'd ask, in the team leads' meeting, what the plan is for the people whose calls the AI takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the easy calls go first, password resets and bill questions, and that's half our volume. If the chatbot takes half the calls, my nine people become four, and four people don't need a team lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to be the one who trains the AI on our hard cases, because that's a role they'd need. I'd take every course the company offers on the new system in the first six months. And I'd push the union for a no-cuts deal for anyone willing to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to grab onto. Like I can see the wave and I've still got time to swim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, honestly, and Mark, who's 50 and doesn't like computers. Priya's young and quick, she'd find something. Mark has a mortgage and nowhere obvious to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said four people don't need a team lead. So where does that leave you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Either running the people who check the bot, or out. That's why I'd put my hand up early, because the people who wait get chosen for them. I'm not brave, I just know how these meetings go.

say: I'd say workers need a **say in the rollout**, not just a memo.
I'd argue the savings shouldn't all go to **shareholders**.
think: The **easy calls**, password resets and bills, are half our volume and go first.
A team cut from **nine to four** might not need me at all.
do: Volunteer to train the AI on our **hardest cases** to stay useful.
Take every **company course** on the new system within six months.
Push the **union** for a no-cuts deal for anyone who retrains.
feel: **Anxious**, but with **time to swim** before the wave lands.
S1.quote: If the chatbot takes half the calls, my nine people become four, and four people don't need a team lead.
fieldNote: He quickly did the maths: **half the calls** gone means his team shrinks to four.
Plans to **volunteer early** for the bot-training role, out of realism rather than bravery.
Worries most about **Mark**, an older colleague with a mortgage and no computer skills.

steps.text: Volunteer to train the support chatbot on the hardest call types
Finish every company course on the new system within six months
Ask the union for a no-cuts deal for staff who retrain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. And robots three years after, but there's nothing for a robot to do in a call centre anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a crisis and the government needs to act like it's a crisis. Online I'd be sharing petitions for a jobs guarantee and a tax on the companies that profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the contact centre closes inside those two years. Answering customers is pure thinking work, there's no hands-on part to buy me time. By 2028 there won't be a phone left in our building that a person needs to answer, and my MBA won't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the gym and anything else that isn't rent, food or my mum's money in the first month. I'd talk to Ana about whether I train as a teacher like her, because a classroom feels more human. And I'd go to every union meeting and every protest about this, because there'd be millions of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like waiting for a phone call with bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the money might stop for a while. That's the conversation I'd dread most. She'd tell me not to worry and then worry herself sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Teaching takes time to train for. Would two years be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, that's the problem. A teaching course is a year, and Ana says the schools would be changing too. I'd be retraining into something that's also moving under my feet.

say: I'd call it a **crisis** and say the government must act like it.
I'd share petitions for a **jobs guarantee** and a tax on AI profits.
think: Answering calls is **pure thinking work**, so nothing buys me the extra three years.
The **contact centre closes** within two years, MBA or not.
do: Cut everything except rent, food and **Mum's money** in the first month.
Look into **teacher training** with Ana's help as a more human job.
Join union meetings and **protests** about job losses.
feel: **Sick**, like waiting for a phone call with bad news.
S2.quote: By 2028 there won't be a phone left in our building that a person needs to answer, and my MBA won't change that.
fieldNote: Understood straight away that the **robot delay** gives his job no extra time.
Most dreads telling his **mum** that the monthly money might stop.
Sees **teaching** as a refuge but knows schools would be changing too.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and the money for his mum
Apply for a one-year teacher training course with Ana's advice
Attend union meetings and protests about the closures

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's 2031, I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a window and we should use it, and I'd say that to my team in our Monday huddle. Online I'd keep pushing for retraining money and protections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough to do a teaching course properly, maybe even part-time while I keep my job. Five years is long enough to retrain, but only if I start the week the news breaks and not the year after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a part-time teaching qualification in the evenings. I'd keep using whatever AI tools the company brings in, because I'd need the job for at least three more years. And I'd try to build up two months of savings so I'm not starting again with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but with a plan, which makes a big difference. I'd still check the company news every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two months of savings on your pay. How would you actually get there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana and I would move to a smaller flat when the lease ends in spring, saving about 150 a month. That and no holidays for a year. It's dull, but it adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Mark and Priya in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get Priya onto whatever new team the bot creates. With Mark, I'd sit with him and help him apply for the council's customer service jobs, because they'd probably be slower to change.

say: I'd tell my team we have a **window** and should use it.
I'd keep pushing publicly for **retraining money** and worker protections.
think: Five years is enough for a **teaching course**, done part-time alongside the job.
It only works if I **start straight away**, not a year later.
do: Start a part-time **teaching qualification** in the evenings within the first year.
Keep using the company's **AI tools** to hold the job for three more years.
Build up **two months of savings** by moving to a smaller flat.
feel: **Nervous**, but a **plan** makes a big difference.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to retrain, but only if I start the week the news breaks and not the year after.
fieldNote: The extra three years turn his worry into a **concrete plan**: part-time teacher training.
Uses the current job as a **bridge**, which makes him lean into the AI tools.
Still thinks of his team: helps **Mark** look at slower-moving council jobs.

steps.text: Start a part-time evening teaching qualification this year
Keep using the company's AI tools to stay useful
Move with Ana to a smaller flat to save 150 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That almost sounds manageable, and I don't trust that feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. At work I'd say let's design the new jobs now, with the people who'll do them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably still leave the contact centre, just more slowly and on my terms. With ten years I can leave the call centre with my head up instead of with a box under my arm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the job for a few years and get really good with the AI tools, because the pay helps us save. Around year three I'd start teacher training. And I'd join a political party for the first time, because the next ten years of rules would matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Not calm, but I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust the manageable feeling. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the offshoring thing taught me that companies say one date and do another. Ten years might be ten years for the country and three for my building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And would anything change with Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably talk about kids sooner, honestly, because a teacher and a trainee teacher is a steadier house than a call centre lead on a rolling contract. That's strange to say, but it's true.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** we'd be fools to waste.
I'd say we should **design new jobs** now, with the people who'll do them.
think: I'd still **leave the contact centre**, just slowly and on my own terms.
Companies **move faster** than national dates, so ten years might be three for us.
do: Stay a few years and get **strong with AI tools** while saving.
Join a **political party** for the first time.
S4.quote: With ten years I can leave the call centre with my head up instead of with a box under my arm.
fieldNote: Distrusts the long timeline because **offshoring talk** taught him firms move faster than announced.
A decade lets him plan **children** with his partner Ana sooner, a surprising turn.
Joins **politics** only in the long scenario, when he sees the rules as winnable.

steps.text: Stay three years and master the company's AI support tools
Begin teacher training around the third year
Join a political party and go to local meetings
Talk with Ana about starting a family sooner

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I couldn't even finish retraining before the work disappeared. What would help is paid time off to retrain and a guarantee that my mum's pension doesn't shrink while I'm doing it. I can handle starting again at 30, but I can't handle telling my mum the 200 a month has stopped.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what customers want. Half my angry callers just want someone to say sorry and mean it. I'm not sure a machine can do that, and I'm not sure companies care.

headlineQuote: I can handle starting again at 30, but I can't handle telling my mum the 200 a month has stopped.
portrait: Carlos, 27, leads a **nine-person support team** at a telecoms contact centre and uses AI tools now and then.
He has **under a month saved**, sends his mum 200 a month, and lives with Ana, a teacher.
He was worried before AI because of **offshoring rumours** at his centre.
He sees his whole job as **thinking work**, so the robot delay gives him no extra time.
More warning moves him from protest towards a real plan: **teacher training** and a political party.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the work would vanish before he could finish retraining.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid time off** to retrain, plus a guarantee his mum's pension doesn't shrink.
